front.title: OAuth 2.0 APM Binding to Entity Attestation Tokens

abstract.t: This document specifies how the Authorization Posture Mechanism (APM) binds to Entity Attestation Tokens (EATs) to provide cryptographically verified device posture evidence within OAuth 2.0 authorization flows. By binding APM posture claims to EAT attestation evidence, authorization servers obtain a tamper-evident, cryptographically signed assertion of the client device's security state at the moment of authorization, enabling fine-grained, zero-trust access decisions.

This binding enables relying parties and authorization servers to enforce posture-based authorization policies with cryptographic assurance, bridging the gap between device attestation and OAuth 2.0 token issuance.

section.name: Introduction
section.t: The Authorization Posture Mechanism (APM), defined in , provides a structured framework for expressing client device security posture within OAuth 2.0 authorization flows. Entity Attestation Tokens (EATs), defined in , provide a compact, signed token format for conveying device attestation evidence from an attester to a verifier. This document defines a binding between APM and EAT so that posture claims carried in APM are cryptographically backed by EAT attestation evidence.

Without this binding, APM posture claims are assertions whose truthfulness depends on the integrity of the channel carrying them. By binding posture claims to EAT evidence, the authorization server can verify that the claimed posture corresponds to a cryptographically attested device state, materially raising the assurance level of posture-based authorization decisions.

section.name: Motivation
section.t: Zero-trust architectures require continuous, verifiable evidence of device security state. OAuth 2.0 authorization servers that issue access tokens based on device posture need stronger assurance than self-asserted posture claims. EAT provides the attestation primitive; APM provides the posture taxonomy and the OAuth integration. This document connects them.

A Cryptographically Relevant Quantum Computer (CRQC) would threaten the classical signatures currently used to protect attestation evidence. This binding is therefore specified to accommodate post-quantum signature algorithms (e.g., ML-DSA ) in the EAT proof layer, ensuring that posture evidence remains verifiable in a post-quantum environment.

section.name: Scope
section.t: This document defines the APM-EAT binding for OAuth 2.0 authorization code and device authorization grant flows. It specifies how an EAT token is presented alongside an APM posture assertion, how the authorization server validates the binding, and how posture claims in the APM map to evidence claims in the EAT. Token formats, signature algorithms, and policy evaluation are referenced from their defining specifications and are not redefined here.

dl.dd: The Authorization Posture Mechanism defined in .
An Entity Attestation Token as defined in .
A structured assertion about a device security property carried in an APM object.
A cryptographically attested property carried in an EAT token.
A hash that cryptographically binds an APM posture assertion to the EAT evidence that supports it.

section.name: Conventions and Definitions
section.t: The key words "MUST", "MUST NOT", "REQUIRED", "SHALL", "SHALL NOT", "SHOULD", "SHOULD NOT", "RECOMMENDED", "NOT RECOMMENDED", "MAY", and "OPTIONAL" in this document are to be interpreted as described in BCP 14 when, and only when, they appear in all capitals as shown here.

section.name: Overview
section.t: In the binding model defined by this document, a client (or an attestation service acting on its behalf) obtains an EAT token from a device attester and presents it to the authorization server as part of an OAuth 2.0 authorization request. The EAT token is referenced from the APM posture object via a binding hash, so that the authorization server can verify that the posture claims are backed by the specific attestation evidence identified by the hash.

The binding is integrity-protecting: the binding hash ensures that the posture claims cannot be separated from the evidence that backs them, and that the evidence cannot be substituted for different evidence after the binding is established.

section.name: Binding Structure
section.t: The APM posture object is extended with an eat_binding member carrying the binding metadata. The structure is expressed in CBOR, consistent with the EAT CBOR encoding .

dl.dd: A hash of the DER or CBOR encoding of the referenced EAT token, computed using the algorithm in eat_hash_alg. This binds the APM posture object to a specific EAT instance.
Identifier for the hash algorithm used in eat_token_ref. MUST be SHA-256 or stronger; SHA-384 is RECOMMENDED. In post-quantum deployments, SHAKE256 is RECOMMENDED.

A list of bindings between individual posture claims in the APM object and evidence claims in the EAT token. Each entry declares which evidence claim supports which posture claim and the mode of matching.

Declares how the posture claim value is evaluated against the evidence claim value. exact requires equality; threshold requires the posture value to meet or exceed the evidence value (for numeric posture scores); superset requires the posture claim to be a superset of the attested evidence.

section.name: EAT Token Presentation
section.t: The EAT token is presented to the authorization server as a separate OAuth 2.0 request parameter named eat, or via a token introspection endpoint extension when the EAT is held by a third-party verifier. The authorization server MUST retrieve or receive the full EAT token whose encoding hashes to the value in eat_token_ref before making an authorization decision.

When presented as a request parameter, the EAT token MUST be a CBOR-encoded EAT (CWT Claim Set) signed using COSE_Sign1 . When the EAT uses a JWT profile, the eat parameter carries the compact-serialized JWT.

section.name: Authorization Server Validation Procedure
section.t: Upon receiving an authorization request carrying an APM posture object with an eat_binding member, the authorization server MUST perform the following validation steps before issuing a token:

ol.li: Verify that the eat_token_ref hash algorithm is acceptable per deployment policy.
Retrieve the EAT token referenced by eat_token_ref.
Compute the hash of the retrieved EAT token encoding using eat_hash_alg and verify it equals eat_token_ref. If the hash does not match, the binding is broken and the request MUST be rejected.
Verify the EAT token signature using the attester's trust anchor. If signature verification fails, the request MUST be rejected.
For each entry in claim_bindings, locate the referenced posture claim in the APM object and the referenced evidence claim in the EAT token.

Evaluate each binding according to its match_mode. If any binding does not satisfy its match condition, the posture claim is unsupported and MUST NOT be used as the basis for an authorization decision.
Verify that the EAT token is within its validity window (not expired, not prematurely used) and that the attestation freshness satisfies deployment policy.

section.t: If all validations succeed, the authorization server MAY use the posture claims referenced by valid bindings as authenticated inputs to its authorization policy evaluation. Posture claims not referenced by any binding remain unverified assertions and SHOULD be treated accordingly.

section.name: Attestation Freshness
section.t: EAT tokens carry attestation evidence captured at a point in time. Posture may change between attestation and authorization. To mitigate staleness, the authorization server SHOULD enforce a maximum attestation age, measured from the EAT issuance time to the authorization request receipt time. The RECOMMENDED maximum age is 300 seconds for high-assurance deployments; deployments MAY define a longer window for lower-assurance use cases.

For stronger freshness, the authorization server MAY issue a nonce in a pre-authorization step and require the EAT token to include that nonce in its evidence claims. The authorization server then verifies the nonce, ensuring the attestation was generated in response to the current authorization request.

section.name: Requirements
section.t: REQ-APM-EAT-1: Binding Hash Required. An APM posture object that claims EAT-backed evidence MUST include an eat_binding member with a valid eat_token_ref.
REQ-APM-EAT-2: Hash Algorithm Strength. The eat_hash_alg MUST be SHA-256 or stronger.
REQ-APM-EAT-3: Signature Verification. The authorization server MUST verify the EAT token signature before trusting any bound posture claim.
REQ-APM-EAT-4: Freshness Enforcement. The authorization server SHOULD enforce a maximum attestation age and MAY require nonce-based freshness for high-assurance deployments.

REQ-APM-EAT-5: Unverified Claim Handling. Posture claims not backed by a valid EAT binding MUST be treated as unverified assertions and SHOULD NOT be used as the sole basis for privileged authorization decisions.

REQ-APM-EAT-6: Post-Quantum Readiness. EAT tokens used in this binding SHOULD support post-quantum signature algorithms (e.g., ML-DSA, SLH-DSA) in the COSE_Sign1 layer to ensure long-term verifiability of attestation evidence.

section.name: Binding Hash Strength
section.t: The security of the APM-EAT binding depends on the collision and preimage resistance of eat_hash_alg. An attacker who can find a second EAT token with the same hash could substitute evidence while preserving the binding. SHA-256 provides 128 bits of collision resistance, which is adequate for current deployments. In post-quantum deployments, SHAKE256 with at least 256 bits of output is RECOMMENDED to preserve security margins against Grover's algorithm.

section.name: Replay and Substitution
section.t: A captured EAT token could be replayed in a later authorization request. The binding hash alone does not prevent replay, because the hash is deterministic. Replay prevention is the responsibility of the freshness mechanisms defined in . Deployments that omit freshness enforcement accept the risk that a stale EAT token may be replayed to support a posture claim that no longer holds.

Substitution of a posture object while reusing a legitimate EAT token is prevented by the binding hash: the hash is computed over the EAT token, not the posture object, so a different posture object referencing the same EAT token must still pass per-claim binding validation. An attacker cannot attach unsupported posture claims to a legitimate EAT token, because the claim_bindings entries are validated against actual evidence claims in the EAT.

section.name: Attester Trust Anchors
section.t: The authorization server must hold trust anchors for the attesters whose EAT tokens it accepts. Compromise of an attester key permits the generation of fraudulent evidence. Deployments SHOULD rotate attester keys and SHOULD distribute attester key compromise via a revocation mechanism. In a post-quantum deployment, attester keys SHOULD use post-quantum algorithms to prevent retrospective forgery.

section.name: Privacy of Attestation Evidence
section.t: EAT tokens may carry device-identifying evidence. The APM-EAT binding does not add additional identifying information, but the EAT itself may reveal hardware serial numbers, firmware versions, or other unique identifiers. Deployments SHOULD use EAT profiles that minimize correlatable identifiers and SHOULD consider unlinkability techniques where supported by the attester.
